Or take the littoral combat ship, which was supposed to be a minesweeper, a vehicle for getting close to shore to insert Special Operations forces, and more. The Navy decided that the ship was ill-suited to a potential conflict with China, because it could not easily defend itself from modern high-speed missiles. But members of Congress from the states where the ships are maintained and repaired blocked the Navy from retiring five of the nine ships it had hoped to terminate.

Meanwhile, the Senate ICBM Coalition , composed of members with Intercontinental Ballistic Missile bases or major ballistic missile work in their states, have passed a law stating that the Air Force cannot reduce the current deployed force of 400 missiles. They did this even though experts such as former Secretary of Defense William Perry have called these missiles “among the most dangerous weapons in the world,” because a president would only have a matter of minutes to decide whether to launch them on warning of an attack, increasing the risk of an accidental nuclear conflict provoked by a false alarm.

To add insult to injury, the new ICBM that is under development by Northrop Grumman, the Sentinel, now has a projected cost more than 80 percent more than original estimates.

Given these realities, one might ask, “how much worse can it get?” The answer is, much worse.

While tech moguls like Musk and Luckey promise to build a new generation of cheaper, more effective weapons, they are also competing for major roles in President Trump’s proposed leak-proof “Golden Dome” missile defense system. Experts ranging from the American Physical Society to the Union of Concerned Scientists to the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists have suggested the dome system would be physically impossible and enormously expensive — a trillion dollars or more over the next three decades, according to an estimate by the conservative American Enterprise Institute.

If executives like Musk and Luckey truly want to create an effective defense for less, they should refuse to work on Golden Dome, which, if fully pursued, could be the greatest boondoggle in the history of Pentagon spending — and that’s saying a lot.

Which brings us back to Project Meridian. Putting major weapons contractors in charge of forging a strategy, that, depending on its main outlines, could greatly enrich their own companies is the height of folly. Neither Musk nor Luckey have any background in geopolitics or defense strategy, unless you count making provocative public statements about “beating China” or pledging to ensure permanent American military dominance through the wonders of technology.

No strategist worthy of the name believes that we can bet our defenses on technology alone. An effective defense force should be grounded on well-trained, well-motivated troops who understand the laws of war and understand that their primary loyalty is to the Constitution, not any single president. Technology is just a tool, not the key to winning conflicts or deterring war.

If we want a genuinely thoughtful assessment of the future of warfare, we should recast Project Meridian with leaders who don’t have a financial stake in its deliberations — one that includes scientists, military personnel who have seen combat, experienced diplomats, academic experts, leaders of industries that don’t do business with the Pentagon, and workers from the arms industry.

Executives like Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey should be treated as vendors whose products we will buy or not based on their performance, as well as their alignment with a smart, realistic security strategy. They are not strategists, and we should not look to them to perform that critical task.

William D. Hartung is principal adviser to the Project on Government Oversight.

articles.title: Astronomers discover second-generation planet made by dying star
articles.summary: Most known planets are first-generation planets, formed when a star is born.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Astronomers have discovered evidence of a second-generation planet found around a white dwarf, according to a new study published in Nature Astronomy.

Researchers focused on white dwarf star HS 0209+0832, the core remnant of a low-mass star that burned through its nuclear fuel.

They discovered chemical signatures indicating the existence of a second-generation planet, a world formed from the cast-off remnants of the dead star.

Most known planets, including those in our solar system, are first-generation planets, which form from material left over when a star is born.

The team used data from NASA’s Hubble Telescope , which contained roughly 100 chemical features from its first observation of the star in 1999 that could not be identified. They identified the chemicals as likely to have come from the material ejected by the star as it died, noting that the elements they discovered could only be formed under the conditions of a dying star. The astronomers theorize that the materials coalesced into a giant gas planet.

The planet is estimated to be a gas giant about the same size as Jupiter, though it’s rapidly losing atmosphere. The astronomers still believe it is likely to survive as the white dwarf cools.

Once the white dwarf maintains a consistent temperature, NASA reported that the planet could remain in a stable habitable zone for millions of years

images.caption: This composite radio and optical image provided by researchers in May 2024 shows IRAS 23077, center, a planet-forming disk, and several surrounding stars. The star at the center of IRAS 23077 is not visible because its light is blocked by its surrounding disk, which is viewed from the side. The diameter of this colossal disk is roughly 3,300 times the distance between Earth and the sun, with enough gas and dust to form super-sized planets in far-flung orbits, the U.S. and German researchers reported in May 2024. (Radio: SAO/ASIAA/SMA/K. Monsch et al; Optical: Pan-STARRS via AP)
